Assignment 02 / Sculpting for Design

Memories in Miniature

Paper boats, school mornings, and a bird with binoculars. Small forms holding very particular memories.

Memory · Sketching · Clay

This assignment begins with childhood recollections and follows them into clay. Medha explored several memories before choosing a familiar lunchbox and a coppersmith barbet as subjects for her sculptures.

01

Before the clay, a memory

One early sketch returns to rainy days with her brother. They would make paper boats, place them in streams of rainwater along the road, and run beside them as they sailed away. The drawing captures an activity and a shared moment, rather than an isolated object.

Other sketches explore school lunches and dance classes. Medha used stacked steel dabbas through much of her schooling; when her mother packed the same lunchbox again during an internship in her home city, the object brought those memories back. Mohiniyattam classes also formed a regular part of her childhood weekends.

02

School mornings, in miniature

The lunchbox sculpture is accompanied by a dosa tawa. Together, they bring two parts of a school morning into the same scene: breakfast at home and the lunch carried away for later.

Medha remembers eating dosa with chutney powder while watching Oggy and the Cockroaches before school. The small clay objects make that recollection tangible. Their value comes from their familiarity and the personal routine they represent.

03

Listening for the coppersmith

Birdwatching is a shared family interest introduced by Medha’s brother. Many family trips revolved around watching birds, and the coppersmith barbet became a particularly recognisable presence.

Its call sounds like a metalworker striking copper. Hearing it would begin a competition between Medha and her brother to see who could spot the bird first. Her drawings explore the bird’s shape before the idea is developed into a sculpture.

04

A bird that watches birds

The sculpted barbet wears a pair of binoculars around its neck. This small addition carries the personal meaning of the piece: the bird is also a reminder of the children who spent hours looking for it.

The different photographs show how the idea reads in three dimensions. The beak, rounded head, tail, and incised surface marks establish the bird’s form, while the binoculars give it an individual character.

05

What the objects remember

The two finished subjects connect to different scales of memory: the daily rhythm of breakfast and school, and the longer hours spent outdoors with family. Both turn ordinary, specific details into objects that can be looked at from every side.

The sketches remain an important part of the project. They preserve the memories considered along the way, including the ones that did not become a finished sculpture.
